title: The Factory That Dreams: 39 AI Agents, No Framework - Rushabh Doshi, Machinecraft

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is a multi-agent operating system with 36 specialist agents, orchestration via Athena, agent meetings that argue to unified answers, and a biological-architecture-inspired harness design. The system runs internal enterprise workflows (sales, quoting, BD, recruitment) for a manufacturing company and is being forked as a general-purpose company-brain architecture at forkmybrain.org. Ira is in daily production running nine go-to-market jobs and is being scaled through the Fork My Brain thesis to other companies. The architecture integrates multi-agent orchestration, layered memory, nightly consolidation cycles, and philosophical guardrails, requiring systems-level understanding. The talk presents a real-world factory deployment with concrete costs, daily jobs, and architectural lessons drawn from a 100-person manufacturing company. summary:
Rushabh Doshi presents the story of Machinecraft, a third-generation Indian thermoforming machinery company, and Ira, the multi-agent AI operating system he built to serve as the company's digital brain. The core problem was institutional memory: decades of customer knowledge, quoting history, and machine customization details lived only in three human heads. Rather than write documentation nobody reads, Rushabh built a system that 'holds' the company's knowledge.

Ira ingests years of quotes, drawings, emails, and schedules—hundreds of gigabytes of private company data—without any model training. Documents are chunked, read by off-the-shelf LLMs, and stored as vectors and relationship graphs. The architecture is biologically inspired: senses identify context, a 'gut' digests documents into facts, layered memory provides continuity, a nightly 'dream' cycle consolidates learning, and an 'immune system' guards against bad information. Evolution spent a billion years solving coherence; Ira copied that homework.

Rather than one mega-prompt, Ira is a pantheon of 36 specialist agents. Athena orchestrates, Prometheus owns sales, Plutus handles pricing, Hephaestus knows machine specs, Vera fact-checks, and Memnon guards corrections so that human fixes stay fixed forever. Agents hold meetings, argue, and produce unified answers—a boardroom that never sleeps and has no ego. The system runs nine daily go-to-market jobs including outbound emails, account briefs, quotations, lead revival, and inbound triage, all from a single Cursor tab. Under the hood: vector and graph databases, a CRM, three model providers, and 213 tools exposed over one protocol. The golden rule is 'Ira drafts, human sends.'

Memory is engineered in layers: working memory, pinned facts, episodic stories, and relationships with warmth tracking from stranger to trusted. A salience gate filters what is worth remembering; corrections always win over stale facts. The nightly dream cycle replays the day, locks in useful knowledge, hunts contradictions, gently forgets junk, and produces a morning report.

Every agent operates under a soul file derived from Jain philosophy: no single source has the whole truth (cross-check before speaking), never state things absolutely (cite documents and dates), do your own job, report truth even when ugly, and nobody works alone. These ancient principles run as guardrails in production.

The economics are striking: an agency quoted $230,000; the system was built for ~$30,000 and runs on a couple thousand dollars monthly with zero training cost. The architecture is now forkable as Brain OS at forkmybrain.org—shipped as an empty nervous system that companies fill with their own truth. The thesis: only you can build your company's brain.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Problem: Institutional Memory in Three Heads
sections.summary: Rushabh introduces Machinecraft, a 100-person Indian thermoforming machinery company. The real company asset is knowledge, not machines—customer identities, quotes, custom tweaks—but for three generations all of it lived in three human brains. The fear was not competitors but forgetting. People leaving meant brain chunks walking out the door.

sections.title: The Concept: Grow a Brain, Not a Chatbot
sections.summary: Rather than documenting knowledge nobody reads, Rushabh proposed growing a brain that holds it—a company twin, not a chatbot. The company makes thermoforming machines serving seven different markets (hydroponic trays, spa bathtubs, EV panels, medical casings, packaging) with seven different buyer types, so the brain had to know which universe each customer inhabits.

sections.title: Ingestion Without Training: Organized Memory
sections.summary: Step one was feeding Ira everything—years of quotes, drawings, schedules, emails, hundreds of gigabytes of private history. No model training, no GPUs, no fine-tuning. Documents were chunked, read by off-the-shelf models, and stored as vectors and relationship graphs. The brain is not a smarter model but well-organized memory.

sections.title: Biology-Inspired Architecture
sections.summary: Ira was designed with a body modeled on biology: senses to identify context, a gut to digest documents into facts, memory, a dream cycle, and an immune system to fight bad information. The rationale: evolution already solved coherence over a billion years, so they copied the homework.

sections.title: The Agent Pantheon: 36 Specialists
sections.summary: Instead of one genius mega-prompt that does everything badly, Ira is a pantheon of 36 specialist agents each with one job. Athena orchestrates, Prometheus owns sales, Plutus does pricing, Hephaestus knows machine specs, Vera fact-checks, and Memnon guards corrections so human fixes stay fixed forever. Agents hold meetings, argue, and produce unified answers—a boardroom that never sleeps with no ego.

sections.title: Daily Jobs, Cursor Cockpit, and the Golden Rule
sections.summary: Ira runs nine concrete daily go-to-market jobs: outbound emails referencing real-world context, account briefs from cross-checked truths, quotations, swipe-left/right outreach, dead lead revival, inbound replies, and company-fit assessment. Everything runs from one Cursor tab. The stack includes vector and graph databases, CRM, three model providers, 213 tools over one protocol, and monitoring. The golden rule: Ira drafts, human sends.

sections.title: Engineered Memory in Layers
sections.summary: A raw language model is a goldfish—brilliant for 30 seconds then it forgets. Ira engineers memory in layers: working memory for recent minutes, pinned facts about who someone is, episodic conversations as stories, relationships with warmth growing from stranger to trusted. A salience gate filters what is worth remembering. When facts disagree, corrections win. Continuity without making things up.

sections.title: The Nightly Dream Cycle
sections.summary: Every night Ira runs a sleep cycle: replays the day, locks in useful knowledge, hunts contradictions, gently forgets stale junk, and turns the day's work into reusable skills. A morning dream report shows what was consolidated, what was let go, and what was figured out overnight. The system literally gets smarter while you sleep.

sections.title: Soul File: Jain Philosophy as Guardrails
sections.summary: Every agent has a conscience—not 'be helpful, be harmless' but a soul file from Jain family business principles. Five ideas become engineering rules: no single source has the whole truth (cross-check before speaking), never say things absolutely (cite document and date), do your own job, report truth even when ugly, and nobody works alone. Ancient philosophy running as guardrails in production.

sections.title: Economics and Fork My Brain Thesis
sections.summary: No training bill—zero. The expensive part was teaching a company to remember itself. An agency quoted $230,000; it was built for ~$30,000, running on a couple thousand dollars monthly. The architecture was pulled out and made forkable as Brain OS: an empty nervous system with agents, memory, dream cycle, and soul file, all blank. Companies pour their own truth in. The thesis: only you can build your company's brain. forkmybrain.org.
